title: Leaving the countryside
hook: High-resolution estimates reveal places gaining and losing people through migration in 2000–2019.
notes: Net migration 2000–2019 from Niva et al. (2023), 'World's human migration patterns in 2000–2019 unveiled by high-resolution data', Nature Human Behaviour 7: 2023–2037 (data: https://zenodo.org/records/7997134, CC BY 4.0). The authors estimate net migration as population change minus births plus deaths, on a 5 arc-minute grid (about 9 km at the equator); it counts moves within a country and across borders alike. Orbis sums the 20 annual rates, averages them into 10-minute cells weighted by population (GHS-POP 2025) and expresses the summed annual rates as percentages; colours stop at ±50%, and cells with fewer than 1,000 residents are left empty. Single cells are noisy and some regional boundaries show as artificial steps: read the patterns, not single pixels. 'Places that lost residents' = 5-minute cells with net out-migration, weighted by modelled GHS-POP 2025 population. Province and state values are the authors' own admin-1 sums; national values come from the authors' country file. The authors' country file has no national value for Australia, so it shows as no data on the national map. The cumulative percentages sum annual rates with changing population denominators; they are not the percentage change from one fixed starting population. Populated-place shares use 5-minute cells with at least 100 modelled residents; the display raster uses a separate 1,000-resident threshold. The source identifies net balances, not the origins and destinations of individual moves.

scenes.title: Twenty years on the move
scenes.text: Red places have positive net migration balances in 2000–2019; blue places have negative balances. The estimates remove natural population change from births and deaths, and include internal and international migration. The colours show summed annual rates, rather than the percentage change from one fixed starting population.

scenes.title: China: from the interior to the coast
scenes.text: China's national cumulative rate was close to zero (+0.2%), while its provincial rates differed sharply. The summed annual rates were +65% in Beijing, +60% in Shanghai and +47% in Tianjin; they were −22% in Chongqing and Guizhou, −18% in Hubei and −17% in Anhui. Switch between the grid and the authors' province estimates.

scenes.title: Europe: the east empties
scenes.text: Romania and Lithuania show widespread negative net migration in 2000–2019. Their cumulative national rates were −9% and −18%. More than four in five of their modelled 2025 residents live in cells with negative balances for that earlier period; Spain, Italy and Britain had positive national rates.

scenes.title: America: the suburbs and the Sun Belt
scenes.text: The US grid shows migration gains around major southern cities and losses in parts of the northeast and Midwest. State-level cumulative rates were +47% in Nevada, +30% in Arizona and +24% in Florida; New York was −10% and Michigan −9%. These sum annual rates, rather than measuring the change from one fixed state population.

scenes.title: What national totals show
scenes.text: National balances mostly reflect international migration because internal moves offset one another. The cumulative rates for 2000–2019 were +11.5% in Spain and +6.6% in Germany, compared with −18% in Lithuania. China (+0.2%) and India (−1%) look almost still at this scale.

scenes.title: What they hide
scenes.text: National totals hide places with different migration balances. About half of the modelled 2025 residents in China and India live in cells with negative net migration over 2000–2019. The US cumulative national rate was +6.5%, yet 55% of its populated cells had negative balances; the corresponding population shares in Romania and Lithuania exceed 80%.

layers.title: People living in places that lost residents to migration, 2000–2019
